name: Z80 (ZX Spectrum)
about: The 8-bit chip in the ZX Spectrum (and the Amstrad CPC, MSX and many more). Written the way sjasmplus and Pasmo (and SkoolKit's skool2asm) write it. Knows the Spectrum's memory map, its ROM routines, system variables and ports.

build._about: How to build code for this chip. With no build command or build.bat, the hint is shown.
build.hint: For Z80 code, set "retroAsm.build.command" to run your assembler, for example sjasmplus "${file}" (or put a build.bat next to the file). To start an emulator afterwards, set "retroAsm.build.runCommand", for example "C:\Fuse\fuse.exe" "${fileDirname}\${fileBasenameNoExtension}.sna" (with a SAVESNA line in the code).

sizing._about: How many bytes each instruction takes. The forms are tried in order on the operands written with no spaces (first match wins); 'only' keeps a form to some instructions. Then the 'extra' bytes are added: IX and IY need one more byte in front, and (IX+n) one more for the n.
sizing.loadNote: With no ORG line, this assumes the code starts at 32768 ($8000), a common place for Spectrum machine code

registers.about: A register is a small store inside the chip. A to L hold one byte each; BC, DE and HL are pairs used together to hold a 16-bit number.

notes.A: The main register: most sums and comparisons work on A.
notes.B: Often the loop counter (DJNZ counts B down).
notes.HL: The main 16-bit pair, usually holding an address. (HL) means the byte it points at.
notes.DE: A 16-bit pair, often the destination address for block copies.
notes.BC: A 16-bit pair, often the byte count for block copies.
notes.SP: The stack pointer: the address of the top of the stack.
notes.IX: An index register: (IX+5) means the byte 5 past where IX points.
notes.IY: An index register: (IY+5) means the byte 5 past where IY points.
notes.F: The flags: zero, carry, sign and so on. Set by sums and comparisons, read by conditional jumps.
notes.AF': The spare copy of A and the flags, swapped in with EX AF,AF'.

NZ.text: the last result was not zero (or the two things compared were different)

Z.text: the last result was zero (or the two things compared were equal)

NC.text: the carry flag is off (after CP: A was the same or bigger)

C.text: the carry flag is on (after CP: A was smaller)

PO.text: parity is odd (or there was no overflow)

PE.text: parity is even (or there was an overflow)

operandForms.text: the {unit} at the address held in {r1}
operandForms.name: Register points at memory
operandForms.help: Brackets round a register pair mean "the memory at the address it holds", not the pair itself.

operandForms.name: Index register plus an offset
operandForms.help: The memory a fixed number of bytes away from where IX or IY points.

operandForms.text: the {unit} at the address held in {r1}
operandForms.name: Register points at memory
operandForms.help: The memory at the address the index register holds.

operandForms.name: Memory at a fixed address
operandForms.help: Brackets mean "the memory at this address". Without brackets you get the number itself.

LD.name: Load
LD.summary: Copies a value from the source into the destination. The source is not changed. Note the order: destination first.
LD.flags: No flags change (apart from LD A,I and LD A,R).
LD.more: Brackets mean memory: `LD A,(HL)` copies the byte at the address held in HL, and `LD HL,(table)` copies the 2 bytes stored at table. A pair is stored low byte first: L goes at the address, H at the next one.

special.text: Copy the interrupt register I into A.
Copy A into the interrupt register I (in interrupt mode 2, I is the top half of the address of the table that says where the interrupt routine is).

EX.name: Exchange
EX.summary: Swaps the contents of two register pairs (or HL with the top of the stack).

special.text: Swap DE and HL (a quick way to move an address from one to the other).
Swap A and the flags with their spare copies.
Swap {2} with the 2 bytes on top of the stack.

EXX.name: Exchange all
EXX.summary: Swaps BC, DE and HL with their three spare copies in one go.
EXX.explain: Swap BC, DE and HL with their spare copies.

PUSH.name: Push
PUSH.summary: Puts a register pair on top of the stack (a pile of saved values). SP moves down by 2.
PUSH.explain: Save {1} on top of the stack.

POP.name: Pop
POP.summary: Takes the top value off the stack into a register pair. SP moves up by 2.
POP.explain: Take the top of the stack into {1}.
POP.flags: No flags change, except POP AF, which takes them off the stack.

ADD.name: Add
ADD.summary: Adds a value to A (or one register pair to another). The answer goes in the first one.
ADD.flags: For A: all flags show the result (Z if it is 0, C if it went past 255). ADD HL (or IX, IY) only changes carry.

ADC.name: Add with carry
ADC.summary: Adds a value, plus 1 more if the carry flag is on. Used to add numbers bigger than one byte, a byte at a time.

explain.1: Add {1}, plus the carry flag, to A.
explain.2: Add {2}, plus the carry flag, to {1}.

ADC.flags: All flags show the result, for the HL form too.

SUB.name: Subtract
SUB.summary: Takes a value away from A. The answer goes in A.
SUB.flags: All flags show the result: Z if it is 0, C if it went below 0.

SBC.name: Subtract with carry
SBC.summary: Takes a value away, and 1 more if the carry flag is on.

explain.1: Subtract {1}, and the carry flag, from A.
explain.2: Subtract {2}, and the carry flag, from {1}.

SBC.flags: All flags show the result, for the HL form too. `AND A` then `SBC HL,DE` is the usual way to subtract DE from HL.

INC.name: Increment
INC.flags: Z and S show the result; carry is not changed. For a pair (BC, DE, HL, SP, IX, IY) no flags change at all.
INC.more: Because INC and DEC on a pair change no flags, `DEC BC` then `JR NZ` doesn't test BC. The usual test is `LD A,B` then `OR C`.

DEC.name: Decrement
DEC.flags: Z and S show the result; carry is not changed. For a pair (BC, DE, HL, SP, IX, IY) no flags change at all.
DEC.more: Because INC and DEC on a pair change no flags, `DEC BC` then `JR NZ` doesn't test BC. The usual test is `LD A,B` then `OR C`.

NEG.name: Negate
NEG.summary: Flips the sign of A: 5 becomes -5.

DAA.name: Decimal adjust
DAA.summary: Tidies up A after adding or subtracting numbers kept as decimal digits (two digits per byte).
DAA.explain: Adjust A so it holds two proper decimal digits.
DAA.flags: Z, carry and parity show the result.

CP.name: Compare
CP.summary: Compares A with a value. Nothing is changed; only the flags are set. Afterwards Z means equal, C means A was smaller.

explain.1: Compare A with {1}. Nothing changes; the next jump decides.
explain.2: Compare {1} with {2}. Nothing changes; the next jump decides.

CP.flags: Z if they are equal. C if A was smaller (counting 0 to 255, no minus numbers), NC if A was the same or bigger.

AND.name: AND
AND.summary: Keeps only the bits of A that are also 1 in the value. `AND A` is a quick way to test whether A is 0.

explain.1: Keep only the bits of A that are 1 in {1}.
explain.2: Keep only the bits of {1} that are 1 in {2}.

AND.flags: Z if the result is 0. Carry is always switched off. P/V shows parity (whether an even number of bits are 1).

special.text: Test A: Z goes on if A is 0. A itself doesn't change, and carry is switched off (often done before SBC HL,..).

OR.name: OR
OR.summary: Switches on in A every bit that is 1 in the value. `OR A` tests A without changing it.

explain.1: Switch on in A the bits that are 1 in {1}.
explain.2: Switch on in {1} the bits that are 1 in {2}.

OR.flags: Z if the result is 0. Carry is always switched off. P/V shows parity (whether an even number of bits are 1).

special.text: Test A: Z goes on if A is 0. A itself doesn't change (and carry is switched off).

XOR.name: Exclusive OR
XOR.summary: Flips in A every bit that is 1 in the value. `XOR A` is the usual quick way to set A to 0.

explain.1: Flip in A the bits that are 1 in {1}.
explain.2: Flip in {1} the bits that are 1 in {2}.

special.text: Set A to 0 (flipping A with itself always gives 0). Carry is switched off too.

XOR.flags: Z if the result is 0. Carry is always switched off. P/V shows parity (whether an even number of bits are 1).

CPL.name: Complement
CPL.flags: Z and carry are not changed.

BIT.name: Test bit
BIT.summary: Looks at one bit. Z flag on means the bit was 0. Bits are numbered 0 (lowest) to 7.
BIT.explain: Test bit {1} of {2} (Z = it was 0, NZ = it was 1).
BIT.flags: Z on if the bit was 0, off if it was 1. Carry is not changed.

CCF.name: Complement carry
CCF.flags: Only carry changes (apart from the little-used H and N).

SCF.name: Set carry
SCF.flags: Only carry changes (apart from the little-used H and N).

RLCA.name: Rotate A left
RLCA.summary: Turns the bits of A one place left. The top bit comes back in at the bottom and is copied to carry.
RLCA.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end. Z and S are not changed (unlike the longer RLC A and friends).

RLA.name: Rotate A left through carry
RLA.summary: Turns the bits of A one place left through the carry flag: carry comes in at the bottom, the top bit goes to carry.
RLA.explain: Rotate A one place left through the carry flag.
RLA.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end. Z and S are not changed (unlike the longer RLC A and friends).

RRCA.name: Rotate A right
RRCA.summary: Turns the bits of A one place right. The bottom bit comes back in at the top and is copied to carry.
RRCA.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end. Z and S are not changed (unlike the longer RLC A and friends).

RRA.name: Rotate A right through carry
RRA.summary: Turns the bits of A one place right through the carry flag.
RRA.explain: Rotate A one place right through the carry flag.
RRA.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end. Z and S are not changed (unlike the longer RLC A and friends).

RLD.name: Rotate digit left
RLD.summary: Moves half-bytes (4 bits) left between A and the byte HL points at. Used for decimal digits.
RLD.explain: Rotate half-bytes left between A and the byte at HL.
RLD.flags: Z, S and parity show the new A; carry is not changed.

RRD.name: Rotate digit right
RRD.summary: Moves half-bytes (4 bits) right between A and the byte HL points at.
RRD.explain: Rotate half-bytes right between A and the byte at HL.
RRD.flags: Z, S and parity show the new A; carry is not changed.

RLC.name: Rotate left
RLC.summary: Turns the bits one place left. The top bit comes back in at the bottom and is copied to carry.
RLC.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end; Z, S and parity show the result.

RL.name: Rotate left through carry
RL.summary: Turns the bits one place left through the carry flag.
RL.explain: Rotate {1} one place left through the carry flag.
RL.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end; Z, S and parity show the result.

RRC.name: Rotate right
RRC.summary: Turns the bits one place right. The bottom bit comes back in at the top and is copied to carry.
RRC.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end; Z, S and parity show the result.

RR.name: Rotate right through carry
RR.summary: Turns the bits one place right through the carry flag.
RR.explain: Rotate {1} one place right through the carry flag.
RR.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end; Z, S and parity show the result.

SLA.name: Shift left
SLA.summary: Slides the bits one place left (doubles the number). The top bit goes to carry.
SLA.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end; Z, S and parity show the result.

SLL.name: Shift left, 1 in at the bottom (unofficial)
SLL.summary: Slides the bits one place left like SLA, but puts a 1 in at the bottom instead of a 0. It is not an official instruction: it works on every real Z80, but some assemblers call it SL1 or SLI, and some don't accept it.
SLL.explain: Shift {1} one place left, putting 1 in at the bottom.
SLL.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end; Z, S and parity show the result.

SRA.name: Shift right, keeping the sign
SRA.summary: Slides the bits one place right (halves the number), keeping the top bit so a negative number stays negative.
SRA.explain: Shift {1} one place right, keeping its sign (halving it).
SRA.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end; Z, S and parity show the result.

SRL.name: Shift right
SRL.summary: Slides the bits one place right (halves the number). A 0 comes in at the top, the bottom bit goes to carry.
SRL.flags: Carry gets the bit that fell off the end; Z, S and parity show the result.

JP.name: Jump
JP.summary: Jumps to an address, anywhere in memory. With a condition, only jumps if it is true.
JP.more: `JP (HL)` jumps to the address held in HL; the brackets don't mean memory here.

special.text: Jump to the address held in HL.
Jump to the address held in IX.
Jump to the address held in IY.

JR.name: Jump relative
JR.summary: A short jump (about 127 bytes either way). One byte smaller than JP. Only NZ, Z, NC and C can be used as conditions.
JR.farText: Use JP instead of JR: it reaches anywhere, and is one byte longer.
JR.more: It can only reach 128 bytes back or 127 ahead (counted from the next instruction). Further away, use JP.

DJNZ.name: Decrement B and jump if not zero
DJNZ.summary: Takes 1 from B, then jumps if B is not 0 yet. The standard way to loop B times.
DJNZ.explain: Take 1 from B, then jump to {1} if B is not 0 yet.
DJNZ.farText: Use DEC B then JP NZ,{target} instead: it reaches anywhere.
DJNZ.more: It can only reach 128 bytes back or 127 ahead (counted from the next instruction).

CALL.name: Call
CALL.summary: Calls a routine. The way back is saved on the stack, and RET comes back.

explain.1: Call the routine {1}. The way back goes on the stack.

RET.name: Return
RET.summary: Returns from a routine: takes the way back off the stack and carries on there.

RETN.name: Return from non-maskable interrupt
RETN.summary: Returns from a non-maskable interrupt routine.
RETN.explain: Return from the non-maskable interrupt routine.

RST.name: Restart
RST.summary: A one-byte CALL to one of 8 fixed addresses at the bottom of memory (0, 8, 16 ... 56). On the Spectrum these are in the ROM: RST 16 ($10) prints the character in A.
RST.explain: Call the routine at {1t}. The way back goes on the stack.

special.text: Call the ROM calculator (FP-CALC, at $0028). The lines after it are not instructions: they are a list of sums for the calculator to work through, ending with the byte $38 (end-calc).

dataAfter.name: the ROM calculator
dataAfter.note: `RST $28` starts the Spectrum's ROM calculator, which reads the bytes after it as a list of sums to do (each byte is one step, such as "divide" or "put 10 on the stack"). The list ends with the byte $38 (end-calc), and normal code carries on after that. A disassembler doesn't know this, so it shows those bytes as instructions. The chip never runs them as instructions.
dataAfter.endNote: This is where the list ends: the $38 at the start of this line is end-calc. A disassembler reads $38 as `JR C`, which is 2 bytes long, so the second byte of this line is really the first byte of the normal code that follows. The lines after this one may be out of step with the real program.

LDI.name: Load and increment
LDI.summary: Copies one byte from where HL points to where DE points, then adds 1 to HL and DE and takes 1 from BC.
LDI.explain: Copy one byte from (HL) to (DE); HL and DE move on, BC counts down.
LDI.flags: P/V is off once BC reaches 0. Z and carry are not changed.

LDIR.name: Load, increment and repeat
LDIR.summary: Copies BC bytes from where HL points to where DE points, working upwards. The standard block copy.
LDIR.explain: Copy BC bytes from (HL) to (DE), working upwards.
LDIR.flags: P/V is off once BC reaches 0. Z and carry are not changed.
LDIR.more: BC = 0 copies 65,536 bytes, not none. `LD HL,start` / `LD DE,start+1` / `LD (HL),0` / `LD BC,count-1` / `LDIR` is the usual way to fill memory with zeros.

LDD.name: Load and decrement
LDD.summary: Copies one byte from where HL points to where DE points, then takes 1 from HL, DE and BC.
LDD.explain: Copy one byte from (HL) to (DE); HL, DE and BC count down.
LDD.flags: P/V is off once BC reaches 0. Z and carry are not changed.

LDDR.name: Load, decrement and repeat
LDDR.summary: Copies BC bytes from where HL points to where DE points, working downwards.
LDDR.explain: Copy BC bytes from (HL) to (DE), working downwards.
LDDR.flags: P/V is off once BC reaches 0. Z and carry are not changed.

CPI.name: Compare and increment
CPI.summary: Compares A with the byte HL points at, then adds 1 to HL and takes 1 from BC.
CPI.explain: Compare A with the byte at (HL); HL moves on, BC counts down.
CPI.flags: Z if A matched the byte. P/V is off once BC reaches 0. Carry is not changed.

CPIR.name: Compare, increment and repeat
CPIR.summary: Searches upwards from HL for a byte equal to A, for at most BC bytes. Z flag on means it was found.
CPIR.explain: Search upwards from (HL) for a byte equal to A, up to BC bytes.
CPIR.flags: Z if A matched the byte. P/V is off once BC reaches 0. Carry is not changed.

CPD.name: Compare and decrement
CPD.summary: Compares A with the byte HL points at, then takes 1 from HL and BC.
CPD.explain: Compare A with the byte at (HL); HL and BC count down.
CPD.flags: Z if A matched the byte. P/V is off once BC reaches 0. Carry is not changed.

CPDR.name: Compare, decrement and repeat
CPDR.summary: Searches downwards from HL for a byte equal to A, for at most BC bytes.
CPDR.explain: Search downwards from (HL) for a byte equal to A, up to BC bytes.
CPDR.flags: Z if A matched the byte. P/V is off once BC reaches 0. Carry is not changed.

IN.name: Input
IN.summary: Reads a byte from a hardware port (keyboard, joystick, tape and so on). With `IN A,(n)` the port number is n with A as its top half; with `IN r,(C)` it is BC.
IN.flags: IN A,(n) changes no flags. IN r,(C) sets Z, S and parity from the byte read.

OUT.name: Output
OUT.summary: Sends a byte to a hardware port (border colour, sound, memory paging and so on). With `OUT (n),A` the port number is n with A as its top half; with `OUT (C),r` it is BC.

INI.name: Input and increment
INI.summary: Reads a byte from port C into the byte HL points at, adds 1 to HL and takes 1 from B.
INI.explain: Reads a byte from port C into the byte HL points at, adds 1 to HL and takes 1 from B.
INI.flags: Z is on once B reaches 0.

INIR.name: Input, increment and repeat
INIR.flags: Z is on once B reaches 0.

IND.name: Input and decrement
IND.summary: Reads a byte from port C into the byte HL points at, takes 1 from HL and B.
IND.explain: Reads a byte from port C into the byte HL points at, takes 1 from HL and B.
IND.flags: Z is on once B reaches 0.

INDR.name: Input, decrement and repeat
INDR.flags: Z is on once B reaches 0.

OUTI.name: Output and increment
OUTI.summary: Sends the byte HL points at to port C, adds 1 to HL and takes 1 from B.
OUTI.explain: Sends the byte HL points at to port C, adds 1 to HL and takes 1 from B.
OUTI.flags: Z is on once B reaches 0.

OTIR.name: Output, increment and repeat
OTIR.flags: Z is on once B reaches 0.

OUTD.name: Output and decrement
OUTD.summary: Sends the byte HL points at to port C, takes 1 from HL and B.
OUTD.explain: Sends the byte HL points at to port C, takes 1 from HL and B.
OUTD.flags: Z is on once B reaches 0.

OTDR.name: Output, decrement and repeat
OTDR.flags: Z is on once B reaches 0.

NOP.name: No operation
NOP.summary: Does nothing, apart from taking a tiny amount of time.
NOP.explain: Do nothing (it just takes a little time).

HALT.name: Halt
HALT.summary: Stops and waits for the next interrupt. Often used to wait for the next screen frame.
HALT.explain: Wait for the next interrupt (on the Spectrum, the start of the next screen frame, 1/50 second).
HALT.more: If interrupts are off (after DI), HALT waits for ever.

DI.name: Disable interrupts
DI.summary: Turns interrupts off: nothing can break into the code. On the Spectrum this also stops the ROM reading the keyboard and counting FRAMES.

EI.name: Enable interrupts
EI.summary: Turns interrupts back on (from after the next instruction).

IM.name: Interrupt mode
IM.summary: Chooses how the chip answers interrupts: mode 0, 1 or 2.
IM.more: The Spectrum normally runs in mode 1: 50 times a second the ROM's routine at $0038 reads the keyboard and counts FRAMES. Games often switch to mode 2 to run their own routine instead (the I register says where to find it).

ORG.name: Origin
ORG.summary: Says where in memory the following code goes.

EQU.name: Equate
EQU.summary: Gives a name to a number. It takes up no memory.

DEFB.name: Define bytes
DEFB.summary: Puts one or more single bytes into the program at this point. Text in quotes puts one byte per letter.

DB.name: Define bytes
DB.summary: Puts one or more single bytes into the program at this point. Text in quotes puts one byte per letter.

DEFW.name: Define words
DEFW.summary: Puts one or more words (2 bytes each, low byte first) into the program at this point.

DW.name: Define words
DW.summary: Puts one or more words (2 bytes each, low byte first) into the program at this point.

DEFM.name: Define message
DEFM.summary: Puts the letters of a piece of text into the program, one byte per letter. Numbers in between are single bytes (DEFM "Hi",13).

DM.name: Define message
DM.summary: Puts the letters of a piece of text into the program, one byte per letter. Numbers in between are single bytes (DEFM "Hi",13).

DEFS.name: Define space
DEFS.summary: Leaves a gap of that many bytes (filled with the second value, or 0).

DS.name: Define space
DS.summary: Leaves a gap of that many bytes (filled with the second value, or 0).

INCLUDE.name: Include another file
INCLUDE.summary: Pulls in another source file at this point.

INCBIN.name: Include a binary file
INCBIN.summary: Pulls in the raw bytes of another file at this point.

END.name: End of program
END.summary: Marks the end of the source. Anything after it is ignored.

BYTE.name: Define bytes
BYTE.summary: Puts one or more single bytes into the program at this point. Text in quotes puts one byte per letter.

WORD.name: Define words
WORD.summary: Puts one or more words (2 bytes each, low byte first) into the program at this point.

DEFD.name: Define double words
DEFD.summary: Puts one or more 4-byte numbers into the program, lowest byte first.

DD.name: Define double words
DD.summary: Puts one or more 4-byte numbers into the program, lowest byte first.

DWORD.name: Define double words
DWORD.summary: Puts one or more 4-byte numbers into the program, lowest byte first.

DZ.name: Define text ending in 0
DZ.summary: Puts the letters of a piece of text into the program, then a 0 byte to mark where it ends.

DC.name: Define text, last letter marked
DC.summary: Puts the letters of a piece of text into the program, with the top bit of the last letter switched on to mark the end (the way the Spectrum ROM stores its words).

BLOCK.name: Define space
BLOCK.summary: Leaves a gap of that many bytes (filled with the value, or 0).

=.name: Set a name
=.summary: Gives a name to a number, like EQU. It takes up no memory.

DEFL.name: Set a name (can change)
DEFL.summary: Gives a name to a number, like EQU, but it may be set again further down.

ALIGN.name: Align
ALIGN.summary: Moves on to the next address that is a multiple of the number (ALIGN 256 starts a new page of 256 bytes, which makes tables quick to read).

BINARY.name: Include a binary file
BINARY.summary: Pulls in the raw bytes of a file (pictures, music, a screen) at this point. Same as INCBIN.

MACRO.name: Macro
MACRO.syntax: MACRO name a,b   or   name MACRO a,b
MACRO.summary: Starts a macro: a named group of lines, up to ENDM. Writing the name later puts a copy of those lines there.

IF.name: Conditional
IF.summary: Assembles the lines up to ELSE or ENDIF only if the sum is not 0.

IFDEF.name: Conditional
IFDEF.summary: Assembles the lines up to ELSE or ENDIF only if the name is defined.

IFNDEF.name: Conditional
IFNDEF.summary: Assembles the lines up to ELSE or ENDIF only if the name is not defined.

ELSE.name: Conditional
ELSE.summary: The other half of an IF.

DUP.name: Repeat
DUP.summary: Repeats the lines up to EDUP that many times. (Addresses after it are marked as rough.)

REPT.name: Repeat
REPT.summary: Repeats the lines up to ENDR that many times. (Addresses after it are marked as rough.)

DEVICE.name: Device
DEVICE.summary: Picks the machine sjasmplus builds for, such as DEVICE ZXSPECTRUM48 or ZXSPECTRUM128. Needed for SAVESNA and SAVETAP.

SLOT.name: Slot
SLOT.summary: sjasmplus: picks which slot of memory PAGE changes (128K).

PAGE.name: Page
PAGE.summary: sjasmplus: puts a 16K bank of a 128K Spectrum into the slot.

SAVESNA.name: Savesna
SAVESNA.summary: sjasmplus: saves a snapshot (.sna) of the program that an emulator can load straight away.

SAVETAP.name: Savetap
SAVETAP.summary: sjasmplus: saves the program as a tape file (.tap).

EMPTYTAP.name: Emptytap
EMPTYTAP.summary: sjasmplus: starts a new, empty tape file.

SAVEBIN.name: Savebin
SAVEBIN.summary: sjasmplus: saves a block of memory as a plain file.

OUTPUT.name: Output
OUTPUT.summary: sjasmplus: names the file the assembled bytes go into.

DISPLAY.name: Display
DISPLAY.summary: sjasmplus: prints a message (or a value) while assembling.

ASSERT.name: Assert
ASSERT.summary: sjasmplus: stops with an error if the sum is 0.

MODULE.name: Module
MODULE.summary: sjasmplus: starts a module; names inside it get the module's name in front (module.name).

STRUCT.name: Struct
STRUCT.summary: sjasmplus: starts the layout of a structure.

OPT.name: Opt
OPT.summary: sjasmplus: changes an option while assembling.

LABELSLIST.name: Labelslist
LABELSLIST.summary: sjasmplus: saves the labels to a file (for an emulator's debugger).

PROC.name: Proc
PROC.summary: Pasmo: starts a block whose LOCAL names are kept inside it.

LOCAL.name: Local
LOCAL.summary: Pasmo: makes names local to the PROC block.

addresses.0000: **START** (ROM routine): Where the Spectrum begins when it is switched on. It turns interrupts off and starts setting up memory; jumping here resets the machine completely.
addresses.0008: **ERROR-1** (ROM routine): Stops with a BASIC error report. Use `RST 8` followed by one data byte holding the report number minus one (e.g. `DEFB 9` gives report A). Control goes back to BASIC and does not return.
addresses.0010: **PRINT-A-1** (ROM routine): Prints one character. A = the character code; it goes to whichever channel is open (open stream 2 with CHAN-OPEN first to print on the main screen). Use it as `RST 16`.
addresses.0018: **GET-CHAR** (ROM routine): Reads the character BASIC is currently looking at (pointed to by CH-ADD), skipping hidden codes, and returns it in A. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.0020: **NEXT-CHAR** (ROM routine): Moves BASIC's reading place on by one and returns the next character in A. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.0028: **FP-CALC** (ROM routine): Starts the ROM calculator. The bytes after `RST 40` are calculator instructions, ending with `$38`, and they work on numbers held on the calculator stack. Mostly used inside BASIC.
addresses.0030: **BC-SPACES** (ROM routine): Makes room in the work space. BC = how many bytes you need; comes back with DE = the first new byte and HL = the last. Mostly used inside BASIC.
addresses.0038: **MASK-INT** (ROM routine): Runs 50 times a second (in interrupt mode 1). It adds one to the FRAMES clock and reads the keyboard. Your own interrupt routine can call it to keep these working.
addresses.0053: **ERROR-2** (ROM routine): The second half of error handling: it notes which error happened, clears the stacks and returns to BASIC to show the report. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.0066: **RESET** (ROM): Runs when the non-maskable interrupt (NMI) line is triggered. It was meant to allow a reset when the NMIADD system variable is zero, but it isn't used on a standard Spectrum.
addresses.0074: **CH-ADD+1** (ROM routine): Moves BASIC's reading place (CH-ADD) on by one and returns the character found there in A. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.007D: **SKIP-OVER** (ROM routine): Helper for GET-CHAR: decides whether a character should be skipped, such as colour codes and the hidden copies of numbers in a BASIC line. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.0095: **TOKENS** (ROM table): The spellings of all the BASIC keywords (tokens), used when printing them. The last letter of each word has bit 7 set to mark its end.
addresses.0205: **KEYTABLE-A** (ROM table): The key tables: lists that turn a key number into the character it produces, with separate lists for the different shift keys and cursor modes.
addresses.028E: **KEY-SCAN** (ROM routine): Reads the keyboard once. Comes back with E = the key number (0 to `$27`, or `$FF` for none) and D = which shift key is held. If too many keys are held the zero flag is cleared.
addresses.02BF: **KEYBOARD** (ROM routine): Run on every interrupt to read the keyboard. When a new key is pressed it puts its code in LAST-K (`$5C08`) and sets bit 5 of FLAGS, so your code can check those.
addresses.031E: **K-TEST** (ROM routine): Turns the key numbers from KEY-SCAN (D and E) into the key's main character, returned in A. Carry is cleared if the key mix makes no sense.
addresses.0333: **K-DECODE** (ROM routine): Works out the final character for a key press, taking into account the cursor mode (K, L, C, E, G) and the shift keys. Returns the code in A. Mostly used inside BASIC.
addresses.03B5: **BEEPER** (ROM routine): Plays a tone on the speaker. DE = how many cycles (pitch in Hz times seconds), HL = a pitch delay of about (437500 / pitch in Hz) - 30. Interrupts are off while it plays.
addresses.03F8: **BEEP** (ROM routine): Carries out the BASIC BEEP command, taking the length and pitch from the calculator stack. From machine code it is easier to call BEEPER directly.
addresses.046E: **SEMITONES** (ROM table): The frequencies of the twelve notes in one octave, stored as five-byte numbers. BEEP uses them to work out a note's pitch.
addresses.04AA: **PROGNAME** (ROM): Leftover code from the ZX81 that was never removed. Nothing on the Spectrum uses it.
addresses.04C2: **SA-BYTES** (ROM routine): Saves a block to tape. A = `$00` for a header or `$FF` for data, IX = start address, DE = length in bytes.
addresses.053F: **SA/LD-RET** (ROM routine): The shared finish for saving and loading: puts the border colour back and checks the BREAK key one last time.
addresses.0556: **LD-BYTES** (ROM routine): Loads a block from tape. A = `$00` for a header or `$FF` for data, IX = where to put it, DE = length. Set carry to load, clear it to verify. Comes back with carry set if all went well.
addresses.05E3: **LD-EDGE-2** (ROM routine): The timing heart of tape loading: waits for the tape signal to change (one or two edges) and measures how long it took. Only used inside the loading code.
addresses.0605: **SAVE-ETC** (ROM routine): Carries out the BASIC SAVE, LOAD, VERIFY and MERGE commands, building the tape header first. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.07CB: **VR-CONTRL** (ROM routine): Part of LOAD and VERIFY: checks a block against memory, or loads CODE and SCREEN$ blocks. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.0802: **LD-BLOCK** (ROM routine): Loads or verifies a data block and stops with a tape loading error if it fails. Shared by the LOAD, VERIFY and MERGE commands.
addresses.0808: **LD-CONTRL** (ROM routine): Part of the LOAD command: makes room for and loads a BASIC program with its variables, or an array. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.08B6: **ME-CONTRL** (ROM routine): Carries out MERGE: loads a program into spare memory, then mixes its lines and variables into the program already there. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.092C: **ME-ENTER** (ROM routine): Part of MERGE: adds one BASIC line or variable to the current program, replacing any with the same number or name. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.0970: **SA-CONTRL** (ROM routine): Part of the SAVE command: shows the start-tape message, waits for a key, then saves the header and the data. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.09A1: **CASSETTE** (ROM table): The tape messages, such as the 'Start tape' prompt and the 'Program:' style names shown when loading. The last letter of each has bit 7 set.
addresses.09F4: **PRINT-OUT** (ROM routine): The printing routine for the screen and printer channels. A = the character, keyword or control code. Normally reached through `RST 16` rather than called directly.
addresses.0A11: **CTRL-CHARS** (ROM table): A small table of jumps for the control codes 6 to 23 (comma, cursor moves, ENTER, colour codes, AT and TAB), saying which routine handles each.
addresses.0A23: **PO-BACK-1** (ROM routine): Handles control code 8: moves the print position one place to the left.
addresses.0A3D: **PO-RIGHT** (ROM routine): Handles control code 9: moves the print position one place to the right without rubbing out what is there.
addresses.0A4F: **PO-ENTER** (ROM routine): Handles code 13 (ENTER): starts a new line. On the printer it sends the line out; on the screen it may scroll first.
addresses.0A5F: **PO-COMMA** (ROM routine): Handles code 6 (a comma in PRINT): moves to the next half-line, column 0 or column 16.
addresses.0A69: **PO-QUEST** (ROM routine): Prints a question mark in place of any code that can't be printed.
addresses.0A6D: **PO-TV-2** (ROM routine): Handles control codes that need extra numbers: INK to OVER take one, AT and TAB take two. For example printing 22, row, column with `RST 16` sets the print position.
addresses.0AD9: **PO-ABLE** (ROM routine): Prints an ordinary printable character, keyword or graphic and then saves the new print position.
addresses.0ADC: **PO-STORE** (ROM routine): Saves the print position in the system variables. B = line, C = column, HL = screen (or printer buffer) address.
addresses.0B03: **PO-FETCH** (ROM routine): Reads the current print position. Comes back with B = line, C = column and HL = the screen (or printer buffer) address.
addresses.0B24: **PO-ANY** (ROM routine): Draws one character at the print position, with separate paths for normal characters, keywords, block graphics and user-defined graphics.
addresses.0BDB: **PO-ATTR** (ROM routine): Sets the colour (attribute) of the character square just printed, using the current temporary colours and OVER/INVERSE settings. HL = the screen address.
addresses.0C0A: **PO-MSG** (ROM routine): Prints a numbered message or keyword from a table. A = the entry number, DE = the table to look in.
addresses.0C3B: **PO-SAVE** (ROM routine): Prints the character in A with `RST 16` while keeping the main registers safe, so it can be used inside other printing code.
addresses.0C41: **PO-SEARCH** (ROM routine): Finds message number A in the table at DE and comes back with DE pointing to its first letter.
addresses.0C55: **PO-SCR** (ROM routine): Checks whether the screen needs to scroll and shows the 'scroll?' prompt when the screen fills. Putting 255 in SCR-CT (`$5C8C`) holds off the prompt.
addresses.0D4D: **TEMPS** (ROM routine): Copies the permanent colours (set by INK, PAPER and so on) into the temporary ones used for printing. No inputs needed.
addresses.0D6B: **CLS** (ROM routine): Clears the whole screen to the permanent colours and resets the lower part. No inputs; open a channel again (e.g. A = 2 then CHAN-OPEN) before printing.
addresses.0DAF: **CL-ALL** (ROM routine): Clears the whole screen and moves the print position back to the top left.
addresses.0DD9: **CL-SET** (ROM routine): Sets the print position. B = line and C = column, both counted the ROM's own way (backwards from the bottom right).
addresses.0DFE: **CL-SC-ALL** (ROM routine): Scrolls the screen up. B = how many lines to scroll.
addresses.0E44: **CL-LINE** (ROM routine): Clears the bottom lines of the screen. B = how many lines to clear.
addresses.0E88: **CL-ATTR** (ROM routine): Finds the colour (attribute) address that matches a screen address, and counts the character squares from a given line down.
addresses.0E9B: **CL-ADDR** (ROM routine): Works out where a text line starts in screen memory. B = line number (the ROM's count, 24 at the top); comes back with HL = the screen address.
addresses.0EAC: **COPY** (ROM routine): Carries out the COPY command: sends the screen, one pixel line at a time, to the ZX Printer.
addresses.0ECD: **COPY-BUFF** (ROM routine): Sends the printer buffer to the ZX Printer and then empties it.
addresses.0EF4: **COPY-LINE** (ROM routine): Sends one pixel line to the ZX Printer. HL = the 32 bytes to print, B = the pixel line number.
addresses.0F2C: **EDITOR** (ROM routine): The line editor used for typing in BASIC lines and answering INPUT. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.0FA0: **EDITKEYS** (ROM table): Table saying which editor routine handles each editing key (EDIT, cursor keys, DELETE, ENTER and so on).
addresses.0FA9: **ED-EDIT** (ROM routine): Handles the EDIT key: brings the current BASIC line down for editing, or clears the reply during INPUT. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.0FF3: **ED-DOWN** (ROM routine): Handles cursor down in the editor: moves the current line marker down the program. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1007: **ED-LEFT** (ROM routine): Handles cursor left in the editor. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.100C: **ED-RIGHT** (ROM routine): Handles cursor right in the editor. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1015: **ED-DELETE** (ROM routine): Handles DELETE in the editor: removes the character to the left of the cursor. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.101E: **ED-IGNORE** (ROM routine): Lets the editor ignore certain key codes. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1024: **ED-ENTER** (ROM routine): Handles ENTER in the editor: finishes editing the line. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1031: **ED-EDGE** (ROM routine): Editor helper that moves the cursor back one place, taking care not to land between a control code and its number. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1059: **ED-UP** (ROM routine): Handles cursor up in the editor: moves the current line marker up the program. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1076: **ED-SYMBOL** (ROM routine): Editor helper for symbol and graphics key codes. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.107F: **ED-ERROR** (ROM routine): Called when the editor hits a problem; it sounds the warning buzz. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1097: **CLEAR-SP** (ROM routine): Clears out the editing area or the work space. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.10A8: **KEY-INPUT** (ROM routine): The input routine for the keyboard channel. Comes back with A = the last key pressed and carry set if there was one; also handles CAPS LOCK and mode changes.
addresses.111D: **ED-COPY** (ROM routine): Prints the line being edited (or typed for INPUT) in the lower part of the screen. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1190: **SET-HL** (ROM routine): Comes back with DE = the first byte and HL = the last byte of the editing area or the work space. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.11A7: **REMOVE-FP** (ROM routine): Removes the hidden copies of numbers from a BASIC line. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.11B7: **NEW** (ROM routine): Carries out the NEW command: wipes the program and variables and sets the system up afresh, keeping the memory above RAMTOP.
addresses.12A2: **MAIN-EXEC** (ROM routine): BASIC's main loop: lets you type lines, runs direct commands and shows the reports. Part of how BASIC works; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1391: **REPORTS** (ROM table): The text of BASIC's error messages, such as "OK" and "Out of memory", one after another. The end of each message is marked by setting the top bit (adding 128) on its last letter.
addresses.1539: **COPYRIGHT** (ROM table): The "© 1982 Sinclair Research Ltd" message shown at the bottom of the screen when the Spectrum is switched on or reset.
addresses.1555: **REPORT-G** (ROM routine): Stops with the error "G No room for line", given when there isn't enough free memory to add a new BASIC line.
addresses.155D: **MAIN-ADD** (ROM routine): Puts a newly typed numbered line into the BASIC program, replacing any old line with the same number. A line number on its own is not stored. Part of BASIC's editor; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.15AF: **CHANINFO** (ROM table): The starting set-up for the four channels: K (keyboard and lower screen), S (main screen), R (workspace) and P (printer). Each one lists its output routine address, its input routine address and its letter. Copied into RAM (CHINFO) at start-up.
addresses.15C4: **REPORT-J** (ROM routine): Stops with the error "J Invalid I/O device". This is the input routine for channels that can't be read from, such as the screen or the printer.
addresses.15C6: **STRMDATA** (ROM table): The starting stream table copied into RAM (STRMS) at start-up. It links streams -3 to 3 to their channels, so for example stream 2 goes to the main screen and stream 3 to the printer.
addresses.15D4: **WAIT-KEY** (ROM routine): Calls the current channel's input routine and waits until it gives back a character, then returns it in `A`. Used by BASIC's editor and INPUT; it relies on the keyboard channel being set up.
addresses.15E6: **INPUT-AD** (ROM routine): Saves the main registers and jumps to the input routine of the current channel, to fetch one character. Mostly used by WAIT-KEY and by INKEY$.
addresses.15EF: **OUT-CODE** (ROM routine): Prints one digit: put a value 0 to 9 in `A` and the matching character '0' to '9' is printed on the current channel. Values 17 to 34 give the letters A to R, used for error report codes.
addresses.1601: **CHAN-OPEN** (ROM routine): Makes a stream the current one, so later printing (RST 16) goes there. Put the stream number in `A`: 2 = main screen, 1 = lower screen, 3 = printer. A very handy routine to call before printing from your own code.
addresses.1615: **CHAN-FLAG** (ROM routine): Sets the system flags to suit the channel that has just been made current (keyboard, screen or printer). `HL` = the channel's entry in the channel table. Normally reached through CHAN-OPEN rather than called directly.
addresses.162D: **CHANCODE** (ROM table): A small look-up table that pairs each channel letter (K, S, P) with the routine that sets the right flags for it. Used by CHAN-FLAG.
addresses.1634: **CHAN-K** (ROM routine): Sets the flags for the keyboard channel, so printing goes to the lower part of the screen (where BASIC shows INPUT and error messages). Reached through CHAN-OPEN.
addresses.1642: **CHAN-S** (ROM routine): Sets the flags for the main screen channel, so printing goes to the upper part of the screen. Reached through CHAN-OPEN.
addresses.164D: **CHAN-P** (ROM routine): Sets the flags for the printer channel, so printing goes to the ZX Printer. Reached through CHAN-OPEN.
addresses.1652: **MAKE-ROOM** (ROM routine): Opens up a gap in memory by moving everything after it upwards, and fixes up BASIC's pointers. This entry makes room for one byte at `HL`; the main MAKE-ROOM entry (3 bytes on) takes the size in `BC`. Mainly for BASIC's own use.
addresses.1664: **POINTERS** (ROM routine): After a block of memory has been added or removed, adjusts every system variable that points past that spot. `BC` = the change in size, `HL` = where it happened. Part of BASIC's memory handling; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.168F: **LINE-ZERO** (ROM routine): Reads a BASIC line number from memory into `DE`. If the bytes at `HL` don't look like a line number it tries the ones at `DE`, and failing that gives line 0. Part of BASIC's editor.
addresses.169E: **RESERVE** (ROM routine): Makes a block of free space at the end of BASIC's workspace. `BC` = how many bytes; `DE` comes back pointing at the start of the new space and `HL` at its end. Normally reached with RST 30 (BC-SPACES).
addresses.16B0: **SET-MIN** (ROM routine): Empties the line being edited and the workspace and calculator areas, putting them back to their smallest size. Part of how BASIC tidies up after each line; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.16D4: **REC-EDIT** (ROM): A short routine to throw away the line being edited. Nothing in the ROM ever calls it.
addresses.16DB: **INDEXER** (ROM routine): Searches a table of two-byte entries for a code. `C` = the code to find, `HL` = the start of the table. If found, the carry flag is set and `HL` points at the entry's second byte.
addresses.16E5: **CLOSE** (ROM routine): Carries out BASIC's CLOSE # command. Streams 0 to 3 can't really be closed; they are simply set back to how they were at start-up.
addresses.1701: **CLOSE-2** (ROM routine): Part of CLOSE #: checks which channel (K, S or P) the stream was using and picks the right closing step from a small table.
addresses.1716: **CLOSESTRM** (ROM table): A small look-up table used by CLOSE #, pairing each channel letter (K, S, P) with its closing routine.
addresses.171C: **CLOSE-STR** (ROM routine): Part of CLOSE #: clears the stream's entry in the stream table so it is no longer linked to any channel.
addresses.171E: **STR-DATA** (ROM routine): Finds a stream's entry in the stream table, taking the stream number from the calculator stack. `BC` comes back with the entry's value and `HL` with its address. Part of OPEN # and CLOSE #.
addresses.1736: **OPEN** (ROM routine): Carries out BASIC's OPEN # command, linking a stream to a channel. The channel letter must be K, S or P (upper or lower case).
addresses.175D: **OPEN-2** (ROM routine): Part of OPEN #: works out which channel letter was given and picks the matching step from a small table.
addresses.177A: **OPENSTRM** (ROM table): A small look-up table used by OPEN #, pairing each channel letter (K, S, P) with the routine that opens it.
addresses.1781: **OPEN-K** (ROM routine): Part of OPEN #: links the stream to the K channel (keyboard and lower screen).
addresses.1785: **OPEN-S** (ROM routine): Part of OPEN #: links the stream to the S channel (the main screen).
addresses.1789: **OPEN-P** (ROM routine): Part of OPEN #: links the stream to the P channel (the printer).
addresses.1793: **CAT-ETC** (ROM routine): Shared routine for CAT, ERASE, FORMAT and MOVE. On a plain Spectrum these just stop with "O Invalid stream"; add-ons such as Interface 1 give them a real job.
addresses.1795: **AUTO-LIST** (ROM routine): Shows a screenful of the BASIC program automatically, for example after you enter a line. Part of BASIC's editor; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.17F5: **LLIST** (ROM routine): Carries out BASIC's LLIST command: switches to the printer stream, then lists the program as LIST does.
addresses.17F9: **LIST** (ROM routine): Carries out BASIC's LIST command, printing the program from a given line number onwards to the main screen (or another stream).
addresses.1855: **OUT-LINE** (ROM routine): Prints one whole BASIC line, including its number, the '>' marker for the current line and any cursor. `HL` = the start of the line. Part of BASIC's listing code.
addresses.18B6: **NUMBER** (ROM routine): While reading through a BASIC line, skips over the hidden 5-byte copy of a number that follows each number you typed. `A` = the character, `HL` = its address.
addresses.18C1: **OUT-FLASH** (ROM routine): Prints a letter as a flashing cursor, such as the K, L, C, E or G mode cursor or the '?' error marker. `A` = the letter. Part of BASIC's editor.
addresses.18E1: **OUT-CURS** (ROM routine): Prints the flashing cursor if the editor has reached the cursor position, choosing the letter for the current mode (K, L, C, E or G). Part of BASIC's editor.
addresses.190F: **LN-FETCH** (ROM routine): Moves a stored line number on to the number of the following line. `HL` = the address of the system variable (S-TOP or E-PPC). Part of BASIC's editor and listing code.
addresses.1925: **OUT-SP-2** (ROM routine): Prints one character or keyword from a BASIC line; called over and over to print a whole line. Part of BASIC's listing code.
addresses.196E: **LINE-ADDR** (ROM routine): Finds a BASIC line in memory. `HL` = the line number. Returns `HL` = its start (or the next line after it if missing), `DE` = the line before, and the zero flag set if the exact line was found.
addresses.1980: **CP-LINES** (ROM routine): Compares the line number in `BC` with the one stored at `HL`. Zero flag set if they match; carry set if `BC` is the larger one.
addresses.1988: **UNUSED** (ROM): A few spare bytes that are never used.
addresses.198B: **EACH-STMT** (ROM routine): Searches a BASIC line for a given statement: `D` = the statement number, or `E` = a keyword code to look for, starting from `HL`. Part of how BASIC runs a program.
addresses.19B8: **NEXT-ONE** (ROM routine): Steps over one BASIC line or one variable. `HL` = its start. Returns `DE` = the start of the next one and `BC` = the length of this one. Copes with every kind of variable.
addresses.19DD: **DIFFER** (ROM routine): Works out the gap between two addresses: `BC` = `HL` minus `DE`, and the two addresses come back swapped. Used by NEXT-ONE and RECLAIM.
addresses.19E5: **RECLAIM-1** (ROM routine): Removes a block of memory and closes up the gap, fixing BASIC's pointers. `DE` = first byte to remove, `HL` = first byte to keep. (RECLAIM-2, 3 bytes on, takes `HL` = start and `BC` = length instead.)
addresses.19FB: **E-LINE-NO** (ROM routine): Reads the line number of the line being edited and returns it in `BC`, or 0 if it has no number (a command typed to run at once). Part of BASIC's editor.
addresses.1A1B: **OUT-NUM-1** (ROM routine): Prints the number in `BC` on the current channel, in decimal. Fine for line numbers and similar; values above 9999 don't print properly. Useful from your own code.
addresses.1A48: **SYNTAX** (ROM table): BASIC's grammar tables: for each of the 50 commands, a description of what must follow it and the address of the routine that carries it out. Used by the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1B17: **LINE-SCAN** (ROM routine): The heart of the BASIC interpreter. This entry checks that a typed line makes sense (syntax checking); the same loop also runs program lines. Not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1B28: **STMT-LOOP** (ROM routine): BASIC's main loop for handling statements one by one until the end of a line. Part of how BASIC runs a program; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1B6F: **SEPARATOR** (ROM routine): Checks that the next character is the expected separator, such as a comma or TO, and gives "Nonsense in BASIC" if not. Part of BASIC's syntax checking.
addresses.1B76: **STMT-RET** (ROM routine): Where each BASIC command returns to when it has finished. It checks for the BREAK key and moves on to the next statement. Part of how BASIC runs a program.
addresses.1B8A: **LINE-RUN** (ROM routine): Starts running (or checking) the line that has just been typed in. Part of how BASIC runs a program; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1B9E: **LINE-NEW** (ROM routine): After a jump such as GO TO, finds where the new line starts in memory. `HL` = the line number. Part of how BASIC runs a program.
addresses.1BB2: **REM** (ROM routine): Carries out BASIC's REM command by simply skipping the rest of the line.
addresses.1BB3: **LINE-END** (ROM routine): Reached at the end of a BASIC line; when running, it moves on to the next line of the program, if there is one. Part of how BASIC runs a program.
addresses.1BBF: **LINE-USE** (ROM routine): Gets a new BASIC line ready to run: records its number as the current line and works out where the following line starts. Part of how BASIC runs a program.
addresses.1BD1: **NEXT-LINE** (ROM routine): Sets up the pointers to carry on with the next line (or the next statement of the same typed-in line). Part of how BASIC runs a program.
addresses.1BEE: **CHECK-END** (ROM routine): Used while checking a line: if the current statement hasn't ended properly it gives an error, otherwise it moves on to the next statement. Part of BASIC's syntax checking.
addresses.1BF4: **STMT-NEXT** (ROM routine): Moves on to the next statement: after a ':' it stays on the same line, after ENTER it goes to the next line, and anything else is an error. Part of how BASIC runs a program.
addresses.1C01: **CMDCLASS** (ROM table): A small table of offsets to the routines that handle each 'class' of command, such as ones that need a number or a variable. Used by the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1C0D: **CLASS-03** (ROM routine): Handles commands that may or may not be followed by a number, such as RUN and RUN 200 (classes 0, 3 and 5). Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1C1F: **CLASS-01** (ROM routine): Handles the variable named in LET, READ or INPUT, finding it or getting ready to create it. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1C22: **VAR-A-1** (ROM routine): Works out where a value is to be stored for LET, READ or INPUT, and whether the variable is a number or a string. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1C4E: **CLASS-02** (ROM routine): Works out the value to be stored by a LET statement. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1C56: **VAL-FET-1** (ROM routine): Works out a value and stores it in the variable chosen earlier, for LET, READ and INPUT. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1C6C: **CLASS-04** (ROM routine): Handles the loop variable named in FOR and NEXT; it must be a single-letter number variable. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1C79: **NEXT-2NUM** (ROM routine): Works out the next two number expressions in a BASIC statement (such as the x and y in PLOT) and leaves them on the calculator stack. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1C96: **CLASS-07** (ROM routine): Makes the current temporary colours permanent; this is in effect the command routine for INK, PAPER, FLASH, BRIGHT, INVERSE and OVER. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1CBE: **CLASS-09** (ROM routine): Sets the default temporary colours (as if FLASH 8; BRIGHT 8; PAPER 8) before PLOT, DRAW or CIRCLE reads any colour items. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1CDB: **CLASS-0B** (ROM routine): Jumps to the tape routine for SAVE, LOAD, VERIFY and MERGE. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1CDE: **FETCH-NUM** (ROM routine): Works out a number following a command, using 0 if there isn't one (as in LIST or RUN on their own). Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1CEE: **STOP** (ROM routine): Carries out BASIC's STOP command by giving the report "9 STOP statement".
addresses.1CF0: **IF-CMD** (ROM routine): Carries out BASIC's IF command: if the condition is true it carries on after THEN, otherwise it skips the rest of the line.
addresses.1D03: **FOR** (ROM routine): Carries out BASIC's FOR command, setting up the loop variable with its limit and STEP, and skipping the loop if it shouldn't run at all.
addresses.1D86: **LOOK-PROG** (ROM routine): Searches the BASIC program for the next DATA, DEF FN or NEXT. `E` = the keyword code, `HL` = where to start; carry clear if found. Part of the BASIC interpreter.
addresses.1DAB: **NEXT** (ROM routine): Carries out BASIC's NEXT command: adds the STEP to the loop variable and, if the limit hasn't been passed, jumps back to just after the FOR.
addresses.1DDA: **NEXT-LOOP** (ROM routine): Checks whether a FOR loop's counter has gone past its end value, allowing for a STEP that counts down. Carry set means the loop is finished. Part of how BASIC runs FOR-NEXT; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1DEC: **READ** (ROM routine): Carries out the BASIC READ command, taking the next values from DATA lines and storing them in variables, one by one. Part of how BASIC runs a program; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1E27: **DATA** (ROM routine): Handles a BASIC DATA line. When checking a typed line it makes sure the items are valid; when the program runs it simply skips over the line. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1E39: **PASS-BY** (ROM routine): Skips past the rest of a DATA or DEF FN statement so the program can carry on with the next statement. Part of how BASIC runs a program; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1E42: **RESTORE** (ROM routine): Carries out RESTORE: sets where the next READ will look for DATA, using the line number given (or 0 if none). Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1E4F: **RANDOMIZE** (ROM routine): Carries out RANDOMIZE: sets the starting point (seed) for random numbers. With 0 it uses the frame counter instead, so the numbers differ each time. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1E5F: **CONTINUE** (ROM routine): Carries out CONTINUE: jumps back to the line and statement where the program last stopped. Part of how BASIC runs a program; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1E67: **GO-TO** (ROM routine): Carries out GO TO: makes the program jump to the given line number next. Also used by RUN and GO SUB. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1E7A: **OUT** (ROM routine): Carries out the BASIC OUT command, sending a byte to a hardware port. In your own code just use the Z80 `OUT` instruction instead.
addresses.1E80: **POKE** (ROM routine): Carries out the BASIC POKE command, putting a byte into a memory address. In your own code a simple `LD (address),A` does the same job.
addresses.1E85: **TWO-PARAM** (ROM routine): Takes two numbers off the calculator stack for OUT and POKE: a byte value in A and an address or port in BC. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1E94: **FIND-INT1** (ROM routine): Takes the last number off the calculator stack and returns it as a whole number: in A here (0-255), or in BC if you enter at FIND-INT2 (1E99, 0-65535). Gives an error if it doesn't fit.
addresses.1EA1: **RUN** (ROM routine): Carries out RUN: jumps to the given line (or the start), then resets DATA reading and clears variables, like RESTORE and CLEAR. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1EAC: **CLEAR** (ROM routine): Carries out CLEAR: wipes all variables, clears the screen and can move RAMTOP (the top of BASIC's memory) to protect space for machine code. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1EED: **GO-SUB** (ROM routine): Carries out GO SUB: remembers where to come back to, then jumps to the given line. Part of how BASIC runs a program; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1F05: **TEST-ROOM** (ROM routine): Checks there is enough free memory for something of size BC. If there isn't, it stops with the 'Out of memory' error. Handy before making room in BASIC's memory areas.
addresses.1F1A: **FREE-MEM** (ROM): Works out roughly how much free memory is left and returns it (as a negative number) in BC. From BASIC, PRINT 65536-USR 7962 shows the free space.
addresses.1F23: **RETURN** (ROM routine): Carries out the BASIC RETURN: goes back to the statement after the last GO SUB. Part of how BASIC runs a program; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.1F3A: **PAUSE** (ROM routine): Carries out PAUSE: waits for the given number of 50ths of a second, or until a key is pressed. PAUSE 0 waits for a key forever. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1F54: **BREAK-KEY** (ROM routine): Tests whether SHIFT and BREAK (SPACE) are both held down. Returns with carry clear if they are, carry set if not. Useful in your own code to let the user stop a loop.
addresses.1F60: **DEF-FN** (ROM routine): Handles a DEF FN line, which defines a user function. Checks it when typed and skips it when the program runs. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1FC3: **UNSTACK-Z** (ROM routine): Used while BASIC is only checking a typed line: it quits the calling routine early so nothing is actually done. Part of BASIC's syntax checking; not for your own code.
addresses.1FC9: **LPRINT** (ROM routine): Carries out PRINT and LPRINT: opens the screen or printer as needed and then prints each item in turn. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1FDF: **PRINT-2** (ROM routine): Works through the list of items after a PRINT, LPRINT or INPUT, printing each one and handling the separators between them. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.1FF5: **PRINT-CR** (ROM routine): Prints a new line (carriage return) as part of a PRINT statement. Part of BASIC's own workings; to start a new line yourself, print code 13 with RST $10.
addresses.1FFC: **PR-ITEM-1** (ROM routine): Prints one item from a PRINT list, working out whether it is AT, TAB, a colour change, a stream change, or a number or text to print. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.203C: **PR-STRING** (ROM routine): Prints BC characters starting at the address in DE.
addresses.2045: **PR-END-Z** (ROM routine): Checks whether a PRINT statement has finished: zero flag set if the current character is `)`, `:` or end of line. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.204E: **PR-POSN-1** (ROM routine): Deals with the separators in a PRINT list: `;`, `,` (move to next half of line) and `'` (new line). Zero flag set if one was found. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2070: **STR-ALTER** (ROM routine): Checks for a `#` stream number in a PRINT, INPUT or LIST and switches output to that stream. Carry set means there was no `#`. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2089: **INPUT** (ROM routine): Carries out INPUT: shows any prompt in the bottom lines of the screen, lets the user type, and stores the answers in variables. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.21B9: **IN-ASSIGN** (ROM routine): Checks and stores the value the user typed for an INPUT. It runs twice: once to check it, once to store it. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.21D6: **IN-CHAN-K** (ROM routine): Checks whether the keyboard channel ('K') is the one in use. Zero flag set if it is. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.21E1: **CO-TEMP** (ROM routine): Handles colour items such as INK, PAPER, FLASH, BRIGHT, INVERSE and OVER, both inside a PRINT and as commands on their own. Part of BASIC's own workings; for your own code, print the colour control codes with RST $10.
addresses.2294: **BORDER** (ROM routine): Carries out BORDER: changes the border colour (0-7) and remembers it in the BORDCR system variable. In your own code, `OUT ($FE),A` with A = colour sets the border directly.
addresses.22AA: **PIXEL-ADD** (ROM routine): Finds where a pixel lives in screen memory. Put B = y (0 is the bottom line, up to 175) and C = x (0-255). Returns HL = screen address and A = which bit in that byte (x mod 8).
addresses.22CB: **POINT-SUB** (ROM routine): Works out the BASIC POINT function: is the pixel at the given x, y in ink (1) or paper (0)? Takes and leaves numbers on the calculator stack.
addresses.22DC: **PLOT** (ROM routine): Carries out PLOT: draws one pixel, taking notice of OVER and INVERSE. Entering at PLOT-SUB (22E5) with B = y and C = x plots a pixel from your own code.
addresses.22E5: **PLOT-SUB** (ROM routine): Plots a pixel: B = y (0 at the bottom), C = x.
addresses.2307: **STK-TO-BC** (ROM routine): Takes two small numbers (0-255) off the calculator stack into B and C, and puts their signs (+1 or -1) in D and E. Used by the drawing commands.
addresses.2314: **STK-TO-A** (ROM routine): Takes one small number (0-255) off the calculator stack into A, with its sign (+1 or -1) in C. Used by the drawing commands.
addresses.2320: **CIRCLE** (ROM routine): Carries out CIRCLE: draws a circle with centre x, y and the given radius, built from short straight lines. Takes its numbers from the calculator stack. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2382: **DRAW** (ROM routine): Carries out DRAW: draws a straight line from the last plotted point, or a curved arc if a third number (the angle) is given. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.247D: **CD-PRMS1** (ROM routine): Works out starting values for CIRCLE and DRAW arcs, such as how many short lines to use. Part of BASIC's own drawing workings; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.24B7: **DRAW-LINE** (ROM routine): Draws a straight line from the last plotted point, moving by the x and y amounts on the calculator stack. Can be used from your own code once those numbers are stacked.
addresses.24BA: **DRAW-LINE** (ROM routine): Draws a line from the last point plotted: B and C = how far to go, D and E = which way (1 or -1).
addresses.24FB: **SCANNING** (ROM routine): Works out the value of the next expression in a BASIC line (a sum, a string, a function and so on) and leaves the answer on the calculator stack. The heart of BASIC's expression handling.
addresses.250F: **S-QUOTE-S** (ROM routine): Checks that a quote mark in a string is properly matched, allowing for doubled "" quotes inside the text. BC counts the string's length. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2522: **S-2-COORD** (ROM routine): Checks that two co-ordinates are given in brackets, for SCREEN$, ATTR and POINT. Zero flag set if only checking syntax. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2530: **SYNTAX-Z** (ROM routine): Tests whether BASIC is only checking a typed line rather than running it. Zero flag set means checking. Used all over BASIC's own code.
addresses.2535: **S-SCRN$-S** (ROM routine): Works out the SCREEN$ function: finds which character is shown at a given line and column by comparing the screen with the character set. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2580: **S-ATTR-S** (ROM routine): Works out the ATTR function: reads the colour (attribute) byte for a given line and column of the screen. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2596: **SCANFUNC** (ROM table): A short lookup table that tells SCANNING which routine to use for things like quotes, brackets, FN, RND, PI, INKEY$, SCREEN$, ATTR and POINT. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.25AF: **S-U-PLUS** (ROM routine): Handles a plus sign in front of a value (as in +5), which simply has no effect. Part of BASIC's expression handling.
addresses.25B3: **S-QUOTE** (ROM routine): Handles a string written in quotes in BASIC, including doubled quote marks inside it, and puts the string on the calculator stack. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.25E8: **S-BRACKET** (ROM routine): Handles an expression inside round brackets, working out the inside first. Part of BASIC's expression handling.
addresses.25F5: **S-FN** (ROM routine): Handles FN (a user-defined function) inside an expression by passing it on to the scanning function routine. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.25F8: **S-RND** (ROM routine): Works out the RND function: makes the next random number between 0 and 1 and updates the seed. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2627: **S-PI** (ROM routine): Puts the value of PI on the calculator stack when an expression uses it. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2634: **S-INKEY$** (ROM routine): Works out the INKEY$ function: returns the key being pressed right now as a string (empty if none), or reads from a stream with INKEY$#. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2668: **S-SCREEN$** (ROM routine): Handles the SCREEN$ function in an expression, checking its two co-ordinates and then finding the character there. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2672: **S-ATTR** (ROM routine): Handles the ATTR function in an expression, checking its two co-ordinates and then reading the colour byte there. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.267B: **S-POINT** (ROM routine): Handles the POINT function in an expression, checking its two co-ordinates and then testing that pixel. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2684: **S-ALPHNUM** (ROM routine): Decides whether the next thing in an expression is a variable name (letter) or a number (digit). A = the character. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.268D: **S-DECIMAL** (ROM routine): Handles a number written in a BASIC line (including BIN numbers): turns it into the Spectrum's 5-byte number form when the line is checked, and fetches it when run. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.26C9: **S-LETTER** (ROM routine): Handles a variable name in an expression: looks up its value and puts it on the calculator stack, then deals with any maths signs that follow, in the right order. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2795: **OPERATORS** (ROM table): A table pairing each maths or comparison sign (+, -, *, /, =, AND, OR and so on) with the calculator action that carries it out and its priority. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.27B0: **PRIORITIES** (ROM table): A table saying which maths signs are done first, for example * before +. Used with the operators table. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.27BD: **S-FN-SBRN** (ROM routine): Works out a user-defined function (FN): finds its DEF FN line, plugs in the values given and calculates the result. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.28AB: **FN-SKPOVR** (ROM routine): Moves HL along a DEF FN line to the next character that isn't a space or hidden code, returning it in A. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.28B2: **LOOK-VARS** (ROM routine): Searches for a variable by name, first in a DEF FN's arguments if inside one, then in the variables area (VARS). Part of BASIC's own workings; not usually called from your own code.
addresses.2951: **STK-F-ARG** (ROM routine): Looks for a variable among the arguments of the DEF FN being worked out, and stacks its value if found. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2996: **STK-VAR** (ROM routine): Finds a string's details, or the address of one item in an array, for a variable that has already been found. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2A52: **SLICING** (ROM routine): Cuts a piece out of a string, as in A$(2 TO 5), and leaves the result on the calculator stack. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2AB1: **STK-STORE** (ROM routine): Puts the 5 values in A, E, D, C and B onto the calculator stack as one item. Mostly used to stack a string's details (A = 0 or 1, DE = start, BC = length).
addresses.2ACC: **INT-EXP1** (ROM routine): Works out the next expression as a whole number in BC and checks it against a limit in HL (used for array and string positions). Carry set means out of range. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2AEE: **DE,(DE+1)** (ROM routine): A tiny helper: loads DE with the 2-byte value stored just after where DE points, and leaves HL pointing past it. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2AF4: **GET-HL×DE** (ROM routine): Multiplies HL by DE, leaving the answer in HL; gives 'Out of memory' if it is too big. Does nothing while only checking a line. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2AFF: **LET** (ROM routine): Stores a value in a variable. Used by LET, READ and INPUT, creating the variable if it is new or replacing the old value. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2BF1: **STK-FETCH** (ROM routine): Takes the last item off the calculator stack into A, E, D, C and B. For a string this gives DE = where the text starts and BC = its length. Very handy with strings from BASIC.
addresses.2C02: **DIM** (ROM routine): Carries out DIM: creates a new number or string array, removing any old one with the same name and filling the new one with 0s or spaces. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2C88: **ALPHANUM** (ROM routine): Tests if the character in A is a letter or a digit. Carry set means it is.
addresses.2C8D: **ALPHA** (ROM routine): Tests if the character in A is a letter (A-Z or a-z). Carry set means it is.
addresses.2C9B: **DEC-TO-FP** (ROM routine): Reads a decimal number written in a BASIC line (or a BIN number) digit by digit and puts its value on the calculator stack. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2D1B: **NUMERIC** (ROM routine): Tests if the character in A is a digit 0-9. Note it works backwards to ALPHA: carry clear means it is a digit.
addresses.2D22: **STK-DIGIT** (ROM routine): If the character in A is a digit, puts its value on the calculator stack; otherwise returns with carry set and does nothing. Part of BASIC's own workings.
addresses.2D28: **STACK-A** (ROM routine): Puts the number in A (0 to 255) on top of the calculator stack as a new number. Handy for passing a byte value to the calculator from your own code.
addresses.2D2B: **STACK-BC** (ROM routine): Puts the number in BC (0 to 65535) on top of the calculator stack, stored in the compact whole-number form. A common way to hand a value from your own code to the calculator or to PRINT-FP.
addresses.2D3B: **INT-TO-FP** (ROM routine): Used while reading a BASIC line: it reads a run of digits one by one and builds the whole number on the calculator stack. Returns with A holding the first character after the digits.
addresses.2D4F: **e-to-fp** (ROM routine): Calculator operation $3C. Takes the number on top of the stack (x) and the power of ten in A (m), and leaves x times 10 to the power m, so it handles numbers written like 1.5E3. Normally used through RST $28.
addresses.2D7F: **INT-FETCH** (ROM routine): Reads a small whole number stored in the 5-byte number at HL. Returns the value in DE and its sign byte in C ($00 plus, $FF minus). The number is left where it is.
addresses.2D8C: **P-INT-STO** (ROM): A second way in to INT-STORE that first marks the value as positive, so you only need DE (the value) and HL (where to write it).
addresses.2D8E: **INT-STORE** (ROM routine): Writes a small whole number into the 5 bytes at HL, using the compact whole-number form. Give it the value in DE and the sign byte in C ($00 plus, $FF minus); HL comes back pointing at the start.
addresses.2DA2: **FP-TO-BC** (ROM routine): Takes the top number off the calculator stack, rounds it to a whole number and returns it in BC (low byte also in A). Carry set means too big to fit; zero flag reset means it was negative.
addresses.2DC1: **LOG(2^A)** (ROM routine): Helper for printing numbers. Works out roughly how many digits a number has before the decimal point (or how many zeros after it), from the power of two given in A. Result comes back in A.
addresses.2DD5: **FP-TO-A** (ROM routine): Takes the top number off the calculator stack and returns it rounded in A. Carry set means it was bigger than 255; zero flag reset means it was negative (A holds the size without the sign).
addresses.2DE3: **PRINT-FP** (ROM routine): Prints the top number on the calculator stack in the usual BASIC style (up to 14 characters) and removes it. Pair it with STACK-BC to print a value from BC to the current channel.
addresses.2F8B: **CA=10×A+C** (ROM routine): Small maths helper used when printing numbers: works out 10 times A plus C. The low byte of the answer comes back in A and the carry-over (high byte) in C.
addresses.2F9B: **PREP-ADD** (ROM routine): Internal step before adding two decimal fractions: gets one number into a form that makes adding easy (negative numbers are flipped into a special form). Returns its size byte (exponent) in A.
addresses.2FBA: **FETCH-TWO** (ROM routine): Internal helper for add, multiply and divide. Copies the two numbers at HL and DE from the calculator stack into the main and spare (alternate) registers so the maths can work on them.
addresses.2FDD: **SHIFT-FP** (ROM routine): Internal helper for adding. Slides the smaller number's digits to the right (A places) so both numbers line up before they are added; if it would slide too far, the number just becomes zero.
addresses.3004: **ADD-BACK** (ROM routine): Internal helper that adds 1 back into a number after its digits were shifted right, rounding it. Sets the zero flag if this rolled all the way over.
addresses.300F: **subtract** (ROM routine): Calculator operation $03. Takes the top two numbers off the stack and leaves the first minus the second (the lower one minus the top one). Normally used through RST $28.
addresses.3014: **addition** (ROM routine): Calculator operation $0F. Takes the top two numbers off the calculator stack and leaves their sum. Normally used through RST $28.
addresses.30A9: **HL=HL×DE** (ROM routine): Multiplies the 16-bit numbers in HL and DE and returns the answer in HL. Only works if the answer fits in 16 bits; checking for a too-big answer is left to the caller.
addresses.30C0: **PREP-M/D** (ROM routine): Internal step before multiplying or dividing. Gets the number at HL ready, works out the sign of the answer in A, and sets carry if the number is zero.
addresses.30CA: **multiply** (ROM routine): Calculator operation $04. Takes the top two numbers off the calculator stack and leaves them multiplied together. Uses a quick shortcut when both are small whole numbers. Normally used through RST $28.
addresses.31AF: **division** (ROM routine): Calculator operation $05. Takes the top two numbers off the stack and leaves the first divided by the second (lower one divided by the top one). Dividing by zero gives an error. Normally used through RST $28.
addresses.3214: **truncate** (ROM routine): Calculator operation $3A. Chops off the part after the decimal point of the top number, moving towards zero, so 2.4 becomes 2 and -2.4 becomes -2. Normally used through RST $28.
addresses.3293: **RE-ST-TWO** (ROM routine): Internal helper: turns the two numbers at HL and DE from the compact whole-number form into full decimal fraction (floating point) form, ready for the maths routines.
addresses.3297: **re-stack** (ROM routine): Calculator operation $3D. Converts the number at HL into the full 5-byte decimal fraction (floating point) form, even if it was stored as a compact whole number. Normally used through RST $28.
addresses.32C5: **CONSTANTS** (ROM table): The calculator's five built-in numbers: zero, one, a half, half of pi and ten, packed in a short form. Put on the stack with calculator codes $A0 to $A4.
addresses.32D7: **CALCADDR** (ROM table): The calculator's list of where each of its 66 operations lives. The code byte after RST $28 picks an entry from this list.
addresses.335B: **CALCULATE** (ROM routine): The calculator itself, reached by RST $28. It reads the code bytes that follow the RST instruction and runs each operation on the calculator stack in turn, until it meets end-calc ($38).
addresses.33A2: **fp-calc-2** (ROM routine): Calculator operation $3B. Runs one operation whose code is given in B (stored in BREG), rather than one written after the RST $28. Used by the BASIC expression code.
addresses.33A9: **TEST-5-SP** (ROM routine): Checks there is room in memory for one more 5-byte number on the calculator stack, and stops with an out of memory error if not. Returns BC = 5.
addresses.33B4: **STACK-NUM** (ROM routine): Copies the 5-byte number at HL onto the top of the calculator stack. Useful for pushing a number you keep in your own memory.
addresses.33C0: **duplicate** (ROM routine): Calculator operation $31. Copies the top number on the calculator stack, so it is there twice. Also used inside the ROM to move a 5-byte number from HL to DE. Normally used through RST $28.
